Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify causes of measurable peripheral mononeuropathies other than carpal tunnel
syndrome and cubital tunnel syndrome.
Assess physical examination, radiographic, and electrodiagnostic findings to identify less
common verifiable peripheral mononeuropathies.
Review nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for less common verifiable peripheral
mononeuropathies.
Posterior Interosseous Nerve Palsy
Overview

Definition: characterized by motor dysfunction of the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN)
Palsy of the muscles innervated by the PIN (extensor carpi radialis brevis [ECRB], extensor
carpi ulnaris, supinator, and digit extensors)
Distinguished from radial tunnel syndrome, which is a pain disorder with no objective findings.
Epidemiology
Annual incidence: 2.1 per 100,000 individuals1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The PIN contains nerve fibers from the C7 and C8 nerve roots.
The radial nerve bifurcates distal to the lateral intermuscular septum, into the PIN and the
sensory branch of the radial nerve (SBRN) within 4 cm of the lateral epicondyle.
The PIN courses under the proximal edge of the supinator (arcade of Frohse) and crosses the
radial shaft.
The PIN innervates the ECRB, supinator, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digitorum communis,
extensor indicis proprius, extensor digiti quinti, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis
longus, and extensor pollicis brevis.
Terminal branches innervate the joint capsule and the intercarpal, radiocarpal, and distal
radioulnar joints.
Etiology
Extrinsic
Proposed sites of compression include the fascia adjacent to the radiocapitellar joint, the
recurrent radial artery (leash of Henry), the tendinous margin of the ECRB, and the leading
edge of the supinator muscle (arcade of Frohse).
Most common proposed etiology, observed in more than 50% of surgically treated cases2
Space-occupying lesions: lipomas, ganglia, and extensive synovitis of the radiocapitellar joint
Intrinsic
Parsonage-Turner syndrome
Spontaneous hourglass constriction (SHGC)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033


Etiology
Extrinsic sources of compression may be known anatomic structures or space-occupying
lesions. Hashizume et al2 treated 31 patients with nontraumatic PIN palsy and reported
that 14 cases were caused by entrapment at the supinator. Of the six space-occupying
lesions identified (19%), four were ganglia, one was a lipoma, and one was a dislocated
radial head. Three patients were diagnosed with Parsonage-Turner syndrome, and two
patients had marked constriction of the nerve of unknown etiology.2
Natural History
Dependent on the etiology of the nerve palsy, with Parsonage-Turner syndrome showing some
capacity for spontaneous recovery
Nerve compression may begin with partial paralysis but lead to irreversible weakness if not
managed as the motor end plates degrade.
Risk Factors
Bulging of the radiocapitellar joint as observed in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, septic
arthritis, and synovial chondromatosis
SHGC has been associated with vasculitis disorders.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Weakness or paralysis of the thumb and finger extensors
Lateral forearm pain is variable.
Pain often precedes paralysis in Parsonage-Turner syndrome.
No sensory deficit
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK

3/38

Weakness of digit and thumb extension (extensor pollicis longus, extensor indicis proprius,
and extensor digitorum communis)
Wrist extension is intact (extensor carpi radialis longus [ECRL] is intact), but radial deviation
may occur (extensor carpi ulnaris affected).
No sensory changes
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Excludes osseous elbow pathology
Computed Tomography
Usually not helpful, except in patients with bony abnormalities
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Used to exclude space-occupying lesions
Also may be used to evaluate continuity of the nerve and denervation changes in forearm
muscles
Ultrasonography
May show evidence of nerve constriction in a static and dynamic fashion
Pathology
Masses cause neuropathy because of direct compression.
In SHGC, hypoperfusion of the nerve is thought to cause intra-fascicular edema, leading to
segmental fibrosis and, ultimately, constriction.
Diagnosis
Nerve conduction velocity/electromyography (EMG) studies demonstrate denervation changes
in muscles innervated by the PIN.
The triceps, brachioradialis, and ECRL are supplied by branches of the radial nerve proper and
are not affected.
SEND FEEDBACK

4/38

Sensory nerve action potentials over the superficial radial nerve are normal in patients with
compressive neuropathy and SHGC but may be abnormal in patients with Parsonage-Turner
syndrome.
Differential Diagnosis
Tendon rupture, particularly that observed in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, is
distinguished by loss of tenodesis effect, whereas loss of digital extension from nerve
pathology will demonstrate a normal tenodesis effect.
Patients with Parsonage-Turner syndrome may present with pain, which precedes weakness
and often is an antecedent event.
Management
Proper management of PIN palsy depends on accurately identifying the cause of the
weakness.
Although initial presentations may be similar, weakness because of Parsonage-Turner
syndrome has a capacity for spontaneous recovery, whereas a space-occupying lesion or other
structural entrapment may lead to progressive weakness that does not resolve without
management. Therefore the threshold for observation differs depending on the suspected
diagnosis.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Known or suspected Parsonage-Turner syndrome
Contraindications
Space-occupying lesions
Structural entrapment identified on imaging studies
Techniques/Procedures
Rest and activity modifications
Consider a splint for dynamic finger extension (so-called low-profile radial nerve brace)

5/38

Stretching to maintain a supple hand
Anti-inflammatory medications
Surgical Management
Indications
Space-occupying lesion
Entrapment identified on imaging studies or nerve without evidence of recovery clinically or on
electrodiagnostic studies
Techniques/Procedures
Multiple surgical approaches and intervals of superficial dissection, including an anterior,
posterior, or lateral approach; approach and site of surgery may be dictated by
ultrasonography or MRI findings.
Space-occupying lesions are addressed.
Complete nerve decompression includes release of the arcade of Frohse, the distal edge of the
supinator, and the fibrous edge of the ECRB; ligation of the arcade of vessels from the radial
recurrent artery (leash of Henry); and release of the fibrous bands superficial to the
radiocapitellar joint (Figure 1).
SEND FEEDBACK

6/38

Figure 1
Intraoperative photograph of a wrist shows the sensory branch of the radial nerve emerging
beneath the fascia between the extensor carpi radialis longus and brachioradialis tendons.
(Courtesy of Nicholas A. Pulos, MD, Rochester, MN.)
A microscope may be used to examine areas of constriction in SHGC, which may be managed
via various options, including external neurolysis, interfascicular neurolysis, or excision and
nerve grafting in severe cases.
Treatment options are a subject of ongoing discussion, with little experimental evidence to
guide treatment recommendations.
These recommendations are mostly based on observation (level V evidence) and opinion.
Tendon transfer should be considered if insufficient recovery of thumb and finger extension is
observed after nonsurgical or surgical management.
Preoperative Planning
Accurate diagnosis guides preoperative planning.
Space-occupying lesions must be addressed.
If concern for SHGC exists, a microscope is helpful to examine the constricted segment of
nerve.
Patient Positioning
Regional or general anesthesia is commonly used.
Typically, the patient is placed in the supine position with the arm on an arm board. A sterile
tourniquet may allow for proximal access to the upper arm.
Surgical Approaches
Extended anterior approach—Through a curvilinear incision across the antecubital fossa, the
radial nerve proper is identified in the interval between the brachialis and brachioradialis.
After innervating the ECRL, the radial nerve divides into the superficial branch of the radial
nerve and the PIN.
Posterior (Thompson) approach—A posterior skin incision in the proximal forearm is made
along the line extending from the lateral epicondyle to the Lister tubercle. Superficial
dissection through the interval between the extensor digitorum communis and the ECRB
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
7/38

reveals the supinator muscle. The PIN is identified under the distal edge of the supinator
muscle.
Lateral approaches—A curvilinear incision along the lateral aspect of the elbow is used to
identify the PIN via retraction of the brachioradialis laterally or via a brachioradialis-splitting
approach.
Postoperative Management
A dedicated period of immobilization is not strictly necessary but may be helpful for wound-
healing purposes and patient comfort. Typically, surgeons may consider a long arm splint for
comfort postoperatively until follow-up at 10 to 14 days.
Although a supervised physical therapy program is not necessary for elbow or forearm
motion, initiation of such programs typically is helpful to ensure maintenance of range of
motion and selective splinting or bracing, with the goal of maintaining a supple hand and wrist
until motor strength improves.
Complications
Infection
Rare and likely occurs at rates similar to those associated with other soft-tissue procedures of
the upper extremity
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Iatrogenic injury to the PIN, including transection and devascularization, has not been
reported but is a theoretic concern.
Other Complications
Patients may report disfiguring scars in conspicuous locations about the proximal forearm.
Outcomes
Accurate rates of spontaneous recovery after nonsurgical management are poorly reported
and complicated by the inclusion of entrapment, Parsonage-Turner syndrome, and SHGC.
SEND FEEDBACK

8/38

Hashizume et al2 reported the results of 17 patients who underwent surgical treatment at a
mean of 2.2 months after the onset of symptoms of PIN entrapment.
16 patients (94%) achieved full recovery of motor function at a mean follow-up of 4.5
months.
Ochi et al3 reported the outcomes of 42 patients with spontaneous PIN palsy without a space-
occupying lesion on preoperative imaging.
Ten of 12 patients treated only via observation achieved Medical Research Council (MRC)
grade 4 or 5 strength, with signs of recovery within 5 months in all but one patient.
Sixteen of 30 patients treated surgically achieved MRC grade 4 or 5 strength.
Better surgical results were observed in patients younger than 50 years and those treated
within 7 months of symptom onset.
Poor motor function after surgical management and in patients who present late in the
disease process may be improved with tendon transfers.
Wartenberg Syndrome
Overview
Definition: radial sensory neuropathy in the distal forearm
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The radial nerve bifurcates distal to the lateral intermuscular septum, into the PIN and the
SBRN within 4 cm of the lateral epicondyle.
The SBRN travels beneath the brachioradialis muscle into the forearm. It penetrates the
forearm fascial between the brachioradialis and the ECRL approximately 5 cm proximal to the
radial styloid.
The SBRN provides sensation to the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and variable sensory
innervation of the dorsal aspects of the thumb, index, and long fingers.
Etiology
Often ascribed to a tight watchband; however, no experimental evidence supports this theory
It may be traumatic, such as with handcuff paresthesia.
Idiopathic neuropathy is ascribed to compression between the brachioradialis and ECRL
tendons in the distal forearm.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
9/38

It also may be iatrogenic. Patients who undergo surgical procedures may experience
superficial radial nerve dysesthesias from injury to the nerve (laceration or neurapraxia) or in
relation to scarring. This may be observed in the setting of closed pinning of distal radius
fractures or in the application of external fixation for distal radius fractures.
Natural History
Spontaneous recovery is common, with 71% of patients achieving good or excellent results
with nonsurgical treatment and time alone.4
Risk Factors
Unclear
Speculation regarding tight bands and repetitive wrist flexion and ulnar deviation; however,
these theories are not yet supported by experimental evidence.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Paresthesia in the dorsoradial aspect of the hand
The paresthesia occasionally may be painful.
Symptoms of Wartenberg syndrome may be confused with de Quervain tendinopathy because
of the proximity of the nerve to the first extensor compartment.
Dissimilar from de Quervain tendinopathy, patients often have paresthesia and pain at rest
regardless of thumb position.
Physical Examination
Dorsoradial cutaneous pain with forearm pronation and wrist ulnar deviation
Altered two-point discrimination (5 mm greater than the contralateral side)
Practically speaking, two-point discrimination is difficult to measure other than on the volar
surfaces of the digits. Therefore, two-point discrimination to evaluate the status of the SBRN
is rarely performed clinically and is of questionable interobserver and intraobserver
reliability.
Tinel sign over the radial sensory nerve
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
10/38

Imaging Studies
Not routinely obtained and typically not necessary; however, ultrasonography may reveal
evidence of nerve compression or neuroma formation in the setting of previous surgical
procedures at or near this site.
Highly dependent on technique and equipment/operator
Diagnosis
This is a clinical diagnosis, and patients rarely benefit from advanced imaging studies or
electrodiagnostic testing.
A radial sensory nerve block will temporarily relieve pain.
Differential Diagnosis
de Quervain tendinopathy: first extensor compartment tendinopathy, which is concomitant in
50% of patients4
Intersection syndrome: brief painful crepitation in which the first compartment tendons cross
the second compartment tendons in the distal forearm.
Occasionally, patients with trapeziometacarpal arthritis or de Quervain tendinopathy have
concomitant irritation of the SBRN.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Mostly considered to be a self-limiting condition, idiopathic radial sensory neuropathy is
managed nonsurgically.
Techniques/Procedures
Resolves with time
Wrist splinting is optional but may be most effective if supination can be maintained.
Alteration of activity is optional.
Corticosteroid injection can be performed at the site of entrapment between the
brachioradialis and ECRL tendons.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
11/38

Surgical Management
Indications
Failure to improve with nonsurgical management
Techniques/Procedures
Requires release of the fascia between the brachioradialis and the ECRL and overlying the
superficial radial sensory nerve (Figure 2).
Figure 2
Intraoperative photograph of a wrist shows complete nerve decompression, which includes
release of the arcade of Frohse, release of the fibrous edge of the extensor carpi radialis
brevis, and ligation of the arcade of vessels from the radial recurrent artery (leash of Henry).
(Courtesy of Nicholas A. Pulos, MD, Rochester, MN.)
Preoperative Planning
Determine the need for first extensor compartment release.
Identify the site of most pronounced Tinel sign in the distal dorsoradial forearm.
May be performed wide-awake with the use of local anesthesia and epinephrine without a
tourniquet
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
12/38

Patient Positioning
Supine with the arm on an arm board; nonsterile tourniquet if performed under local
anesthesia without epinephrine or general or regional anesthesia
Surgical Approaches
A longitudinal incision is made volar to the site of the maximum Tinel sign.
The fascia between the brachioradialis and the ECRL tendon is released to identify the
superficial radial sensory nerve.
Postoperative Management
A soft dressing is applied postoperatively.
Unrestricted range of motion is permitted at the first postoperative visit.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Care must be taken to protect the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve in the subcutaneous
fat during superficial dissection.
A portion of the brachioradialis tendon may be incised to adequately decompress the
superficial radial sensory nerve.
Complications
Infection
Rare and likely occurs at rates similar to those associated with other soft-tissue procedures of
the upper extremity
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve branch may be injured during superficial dissection.
Other Complications
Ensure that de Quervain tendinopathy is adequately addressed at the time of surgical
management, if indicated
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
13/38

Outcomes
Lanzetta and Foucher4 treated 29 cases of Wartenberg syndrome nonsurgically via removal of
tight watches or bands and splint immobilization.
Good or excellent results were achieved in 71% of patients within the study period.
Only 3 of 29 patients received a corticosteroid injection.
Dellon and Mackinnon5 described 35 patients who underwent surgical treatment after 6
months of nonsurgical treatment, with good or excellent outcomes reported in 86%.
Without simulated surgery controls, whether these results are better than nonspecific effects
(time, self-limiting course, placebo effects) remains unclear.
Anterior Interosseous Nerve Palsy
Overview
Definition: isolated dysfunction of the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) branch of the median
nerve
Epidemiology
Less than 1% of all upper extremity peripheral neuropathies
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The AIN contains nerve fibers from C8 and T1 nerve roots.
The AIN branches from the median nerve, 4 to 6 cm distal to the elbow; travels between the
flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) initially, then between
the flexor pollicis longus (FPL) and the FDP; and subsequently lies on the anterior surface of
the interosseous membrane, traveling with the anterior interosseous artery to the pronator
quadratus.
The AIN innervates the FPL and the FDP to the index and long fingers and the pronator
quadratus.
Terminal branches innervate the joint capsule of the radiocarpal, intercarpal,
carpometacarpal, and distal radioulnar joints.
Etiology

14/38

Proposed sites of compression include fibrous bands from the deep (most common) or
superficial head of the pronator teres, fibrous arcade of the FDS, and aberrant muscles (flexor
carpi radialis, Gantzer [accessory head of the FPL], palmaris profundus, accessory muscles
from the FDS to the FDP and the flexor carpi radialis brevis).
Parsonage-Turner syndrome
Natural History
Most commonly a transient idiopathic nerve palsy rather than a compressive neuropathy
Most patients improve without surgical treatment.6
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
May occur spontaneously
Difficulty with pinch, writing activity
Presents as varying degrees of weakness
Occasionally, the FDP to the long or index finger is not involved, making distinction from FPL
rupture important.
No sensory loss
Physical Examination
Loss of function of the FPL and FDP (inability to make a circle with the index finger and thumb
[the O sign])
Long FDP may be spared because of innervation from the ulnar nerve.
Patients with Martin-Gruber connections (median to the AIN connection to the ulnar nerve at
the forearm) may present with intrinsic weakness (15% to 39% of patients).
Intact FPL tenodesis
Sensibility unaffected
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Not routine
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
15/38

Consider an elbow radiograph to rule out supracondyloid process.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Rarely indicated unless concern for space-occupying lesion exists
Findings
FPL/FDP muscle edema/atrophy
AIN edema/intraneural changes
Ultrasonography
Able to identify SHGC7
Diagnosis
Electrodiagnostic testing: denervation changes in the FPL and the pronator quadratus with
sparing of the pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, abductor pollicis brevis muscles, and
ulnar/radial nerve–innervated C7 and C8 muscles
Routine median nerve motor conduction studies (with recording electrodes over the abductor
pollicis brevis) are normal.
Median nerve sensory conduction studies are normal.
Differentiate from brachial plexus neuritis via EMG of the shoulder girdle.
Differential Diagnosis
Parsonage-Turner syndrome, which often has preceding pain in the affected extremity and
may occur after viral illness or other triggers
AIN may be a variant of Parsonage-Turner syndrome.
Cervical radiculopathy
Thoracic outlet compression (TOC)
Mannerfelt syndrome (FPL rupture), distinguished by lack of tenodesis effect of the thumb
interphalangeal joint
Management
Nonsurgical Management

Indications
First-line treatment for AIN palsy
Contraindications
Space-occupying lesion identified on imaging studies
Techniques/Procedures
Primarily observation with repeated examinations
Surgical Management
Indications
Space-occupying lesion
Surgical exploration is a treatment option for idiopathic AIN.
AIN palsy usually is self-limiting and may improve for as long as 18 months; therefore, a time
criterion for considering surgical management is difficult to determine.
Techniques/Procedures
Includes release of the lacertus fibrosus, release of the superficial arch of the FDS, detachment
of the superficial head of the pronator teres, ligation of any crossing vessels, and removal of
any space-occupying lesions
If no apparent compression is identified, intraneural examination should be considered with
epineurotomy and internal neurolysis.
Preoperative Planning
Space-occupying lesions identified via three-dimensional imaging studies must be addressed.
A microscope should be available to examine any constricted segment of the nerve.
Patient Positioning
Regional anesthesia
Supine with the arm on an arm board; sterile tourniquet.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
17/38

Surgical Approaches
Via a curvilinear incision in the proximal forearm, the lacertus fibrosis is divided, and the
pronator teres tendon is identified between the radial sensory nerve and the radial vessels.
After releasing or lengthening the pronator teres tendon, the median nerve is identified in the
proximal forearm ulnar to the brachial artery and vein.
Postoperative Management
No specific reason exits for immobilization postoperatively other than wound healing and
patient comfort unless the pronator teres is lengthened.
If the muscle is lengthened, the elbow and wrist are immobilized for 10 to 14 days
postoperatively.
Strengthening may begin by 6 weeks postoperatively if a step-cut lengthening of the pronator
teres is performed.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Ensure adequate release of all potential sites of compression
Surgeons should be prepared to examine constricted segments of the nerve if no site of
compression is identified.
Complications
Infection
Rare and likely occurs at rates similar to those associated with other soft-tissue procedures of
the upper extremity
Outcomes
Seki et al8 observed 21 patients with spontaneous AIN palsy.
All 15 patients with FDP palsy recovered to MRC grade 4 strength or better.
Most (16 of 18) patients with FPL palsy recovered to MRC grade 4 strength or better.
Time to first signs of recovery ranged from 1 to 24 months.
Sood and Burke9 compared the results of nonsurgical and surgical management of 19 AIN
palsies.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Less Common Objectively Verifiable Peripheral Mononeuropathies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
18/38

Seven of eight limbs managed surgically achieved a good result.
Eight of 11 limbs managed via observation achieved a good result.
Time to achieve the final result was similar between the two groups.
Ulnar Tunnel Syndrome
Overview
Definition: ulnar neuropathy at or distal to the wrist
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Contains nerve fibers from C8 and T1 nerve roots
Approximately 4.0 to 4.5 cm long
Spans from the proximal edge of the volar carpal ligament to the distal margin of the fibrous
arch of the hypothenar muscles
The division of the ulnar nerve into the superficial sensory and deep motor branches in the
Guyon canal allows the canal to be divided into three zones (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3

Illustration of a wrist shows the anatomy of the Guyon canal and potential sites of
compression. (Courtesy of Michael Lin, MD, PhD, Orange, CA.)
Figure 4
Illustration of a wrist shows the three zones of the Guyon canal. The palmaris brevis is omitted
for clarity. (Courtesy of Michael Lin, MD, PhD, Orange, CA.)
Osteology
Floor: flexor retinaculum and muscles of the hypothenar eminence (proximally), pisohamate
and pisometacarpal ligaments (distally)
Radial border: hook of the hamate
Ulnar border: pisiform and abductor digiti minimi
Roof: volar carpal ligament (continuation of deep forearm fascia and fibrous arcade that
connects the hook of the hamate and the pisiform ligament) and palmaris brevis
Vascular Anatomy
The ulnar artery travels radial to the ulnar nerve in zone 1 before continuing as the superficial
palmar arch.
Nerves
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004033
20/38

Zone 1: proximal to the nerve bifurcation into motor and sensory branches; the nerve lies
ulnar to the artery in this zone. Compression produces mixed sensory and motor symptoms.
Zone 2: includes the deep motor branch as it courses ulnarward into the pisohamate hiatus to
just beyond the fibrous arch of the hypothenar muscles; compression here produces purely
motor symptoms. Affected muscles include the flexor pollicis brevis and all the intrinsic
muscles except the radial two lumbricals (median nerve innervated; Figure 5).
Figure 5
Schematic drawing of the distal ulnar tunnel shows the locations of the three zones: Zone 1
(coarse stippling), zone 2 (lines), zone 3 (fine stippling). A = ulnar artery, H = hamulus, N = ulnar
nerve, P = pisiform. (Reproduced with permission from Gross MS, Gelberman RH: The anatomy
of the distal ulnar tunnel. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1985;196:238-247.)
Zone 3: includes the superficial branch or the sensory component; compression here produces
purely sensory symptoms.
Etiology
Zone 1: ganglia most common
Zone 2: ganglia most common
Zone 3: ulnar artery thrombosis or aneurysm (hypothenar hammer syndrome) most common
Other space-occupying lesions (lipoma)
Bony anomalies (hook of the hamate fracture, pisiform dislocation)

Repeated trauma
Idiopathic, speculated to be related to fibrous bands (fascia of the palmaris brevis, aponeurotic
arch of the hypothenar muscles, thickened pisohamate ligament, palmar carpal ligament,
congenital bands)
Traumatic adhesions
Hypertrophy of overlying palmaris brevis
Anomalous muscles
Inflammatory arthritis
Natural History
Nonsurgical management results in resolution in more than 90% of cases.10
Risk Factors
Workers who experience repetitive blunt force to the hypothenar eminence
Racquet sports
Bicyclists
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Numbness/tingling in the ring and little fingers
Weakness of grip strength
Loss of dexterity
Ulnar palm and dorsal hand feel normal.

This section reviews TOC documented by measurable pathology or objective findings on
electrodiagnostic or vascular studies. Speculative TOS or conditions with no objectively
verifiable pathology are not reviewed.

Abnormal electrodiagnostic studies
Venous or arterial thrombosis
Conversely, most patients diagnosed with TOC have no objective findings on imaging or
electrodiagnostic studies, so-called electrodiagnostically normal TOC.

Costoclavicular space
Bordered by the clavicle, subclavius muscle, and costocoracoid ligament anteriorly; the first

For patients with speculative pathology, natural history is difficult to study experimentally.
